Ever since Nigel Tufnel showed off his Marshall amp that goes to 11, it's been very popular for everyone involved in music to just "crank it up and tear the knob off." This has crossed over to DJing, and I've seen many DJs just have all their levels up all the way, with the meters firmly in the red. There may be some value to that as a lead guitarist, but as a DJ is just leads to muddied sound. This article will explain why.

What is clipping?

Clipping is when the audio output is pushed beyond the capability of the amplifier. Normally when music is produced, the sound will create a smooth wave that flows smoothly from the top of the axis to the bottom. This translates into the speaker cone moving back and forth with the same smoothness. An amplifier will try to draw as much current as is called for even if other parts of the system can't handle it. When this happens, the waveform is expanded past the point that the rest of the system is capable of managing, and the waveform gets its curves 'clipped' off at the top and bottom. This is why we call it clipping. Professional audio equipment will always include an indicator that shows how much signal power is being output in relation to what the amplifier is capable of.

Why is it bad?

When an audio wave is clipped, that translates into the speaker not moving back and forth as smoothly as it needs to in order to re-create the sound faithfully. This will cause the sound to distort, sometimes painfully, and your audience will be disappointed. Of course, some musicians (and even some DJs) will deliberately introduce distortion in order to create a specific quality to the sound, but this is usually done in a controlled manner so that the difference in volume between the distorted and undistorted sound is not jarring to the listener. For the most part, as a DJ you're going to want everything played at the same volume.

If you are spinning at a nightclub, a big outdoor venue, or even in your bedroom, your decks or controller are at the very beginning of the signal chain. As such, they need to have the cleanest possible sound because any distortion introduced at the deck level will be amplified in every device along the signal chain, all the way to the speakers. If you're in a nightclub environment, you will likely only have control of the first 2-3 stages of the signal chain, and the venue's sound person will control the rest. If the signal you send to them is clipped and distorting, there is no amount of tweaking they can do to 'unclip' it. It's tempting to turn your levels up if you think your sound is too low, but it's better to (politely) ask the sound engineer for more volume at the end of the signal chain rather than trying to push it at the beginning.

If you are using a self-contained setup, like a mobile DJ would use, the same rules apply, but since you have control over the whole signal chain, it's better to make sure things are relatively low and clean at the beginning of the chain and just use your final amplifier to determine the volume in the room. If things are so low that your final volume is inadequate in the room, you can move up the signal chain one component at a time to see how much more volume you can get out of it before clipping sets in. If you do it this way, even if you put a surprisingly loud track on, it won't freak out the crowd, and you can lower it from your decks or first mixer without having to run through all the other components.

Duh! Why did you write this?

You would be surprised how many times I've seen DJs and musicians alike not know why their setup sounds like shit, and when I glance at their equipment, I see all their faders and knobs pegged with the needles or LEDs pretty far in the red. It just seems to be a "rockstar" thing to do, and I was also guilty of it before an unusually friendly soundman explained most of what I've written above. Without that talk, I might still be pissing off sound people and not knowing it. In fact, I'm pretty sure I owe whoever the DNA Lounge's sound guy was in 2005 a beer.

Parts:

Labour:
In the the same article, dictates that it costs $4.00 in labour to build the device. Based on another article found here, Foxconn workers make on average $1.50-$2.20 per hour. The federal minimum wage in the USA is $7.25 and this would bring up the production cost to $14.50. This of course is taking some liberties and assuming a great deal. Then there's things like mandatory breaks, overtime etc.. None of which I would imagine are an issue in China.
